examples.knowledge_point: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Integral Containing a Single Logarithmic Factor
examples.worked_solution:
At first, it may not look like we have two factors. Actually, we do, but one of them is implicit. The trick is to write the integral as

$$
\int \ln{x}\,\textrm{d}x = \int \ln{x} \cdot 1 \cdot \textrm{d}x.
$$

 

Using this trick, we can now use integration by parts. We let

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the by-parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+C \\  & =x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{4}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ {v}^{′}=\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{4}⁡(2x)}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={log}_{4}⁡(2x)\cdot (-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}})-\int (-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{log}_{4}⁡(2x)}{3{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{log}_{4}⁡(2x)}{3{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}})+C \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-\frac{1}{9{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C \\  & =-\frac{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1}{9{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{4}⁡(2x)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}.$
